page: The UpCloud STARTER-2xCPU-16GB is a virtual server instance belonging to the Starter family, running on the KVM hypervisor. It features an x86_64 AMD EPYC 9575F processor operating at 2.0 GHz, configured with 2 physical cores and 2 vCPUs under a shared allocation model. The system is equipped with 16.0 GB of RAM, providing a high memory-to-vCPU ratio of 8.0 GB per core. Local storage is provided via a bundled 50 GB SSD, and the instance includes one complimentary public IPv4 address. The CPU architecture supports advanced instruction sets, including AVX-512 vector extensions, AVX_VNNI, and hardware-accelerated cryptography features such as AES and SHA_NI.

Benchmark data reveals a stark contrast between single-core and multi-core performance. Single-core execution is highly competitive, with stress-ng single-core CPU performance and single-threaded gzip compression both ranking in the top tier. Similarly, single-threaded bzip3 decompression reaches top-tier speeds. However, multi-threaded and multi-core operations show limitations, likely due to the shared CPU allocation. The stress-ng multi-core CPU score falls into the average category, while the PassMark CPU score and multi-threaded bzip3 decompression are positioned in the weak bottom 25%. Memory bandwidth remains moderate, with large-block read and write speeds averaging in the middle tier.

This hardware profile offers qualitative cost efficiency for memory-intensive workloads that do not require sustained, dedicated multi-core CPU performance. While database operations and Redis SET benchmarks register in the lower 25th percentile, the generous 16.0 GB RAM allocation relative to the 2 vCPUs makes it suitable for memory-heavy, low-CPU tasks. It is well-suited for static web serving, which achieves average throughput, as well as lightweight LLM inference tasks using small models. However, the shared CPU model and poor performance on medium-sized LLM models make it unsuitable for intensive parallel processing, large-scale machine learning, or heavy database workloads.
